lines.text: You come in late and dripping, near MossHome, the bigfoot town. A flood-warden in very tall boots hands you a jar of mosslight.
"Happens every season,"
says the warden.
"Not usually to this many."
A bigfoot jogs toward you with knotted cords. The path folds up in front of her, and she jogs in place.
"MossHome runner! Third missing path today!"
she puffs.
"Help me find it?"
All the ferns along one side are leaning the same way, like people pointing. You follow them, and there's the path, only a little way over, sulking behind a holly bush. The runner whoops.
"MossHome is north!"
she calls, jogging off.
"Come and see us! Bring your feet!"
You find a path. It is the wrong one, and it walks you in a neat circle back to the runner, who has found the right one herself while you were gone and is jogging in place, laughing.
"Happens to everybody this season,"
she puffs, and jogs away north.
You carry a bundle of cords to the bend. Every knot marks a moved path.
"Forest likes records,"
says the runner. When the way opens, she jogs north, tying another knot.
Your bigfoot knocks twice on a trunk and jogs alongside her. The folded path shakes out like a blanket.
"Haven't seen a knock like that outside town!"
puffs the runner.
"MossHome's north. Visit!"
"Here!"
The trees count your packs anyway: socks, crumbs, anything that hums. At last a path opens, like a teacher closing a book.
Paths open ahead of you and close behind three prospectors, whose pockets hum.
"That hedge is new!"
shouts the boggart prospector, as they walk straight into one. The forest is checking what people carry.
A hedge holds the prospectors by their coats.
"We only took what fell!"
shouts one. Their pockets hum. Nobody gets left in a hedge.
The prospectors empty their humming pockets. The hedge lets go of their coats, one at a time.
"Oh,"
says the loudest. The hedge rustles a satisfied tsk.
Two unicorns tend a gray glade.
"We are mending,"
says the elder.
"Will you help?"
Pass the mending hum along the moss, or guard the edge and learn the woodland's pattern of sounds. The worst glade, farther north, will need one or the other.
You tell them about the crumb you pressed down and its green shoot. The elder's ears go straight up.
"Down,"
she says.
"Not away. Down."
She lets you start the mending hum. The moss greens from the middle out.
When the glade is quiet, the elder rests her horn where the stone fell.
"These stones are not of the mountain,"
she says.
"The forest remembers them from before the mountain had its name."
She says nothing more. Then, quieter:
"This was a small one. The worst glade is north of here."
The elder touches the ground with one hoof.
"Before names,"
she says. That is all she will say.
"Slowly,"
says the elder.
"The forest dislikes hurry. Something in the worst glade listens for loud things. Go quiet, or go so noisy it can't follow."
That is a lot of words, for her.
A huge beech has sat down across the path, roots tucked under like a grandpa's feet.
"Why did you come?"
it whispers. A squirrel taps on its shoulder, impatient.
"The stones,"
you say. The beech is quiet so long the squirrel falls asleep.
"Honest,"
it whispers at last, and shuffles aside.
"Go gently. The glade is sore, and something there is listening."
"Passing through,"
the beech repeats slowly.
"Everybody is passing through. Even me. I am just slower."
It gets up one root at a time, which takes as long as eating a cookie, and waves you on.
"To find out,"
the beech repeats, and every leaf rustles, pleased.
"Curious. Good."
It stands up quite fast, for a beech, and drops a leaf on your shoulder: look closely in there.
"We told the roll call everything,"
you remind it. The beech creaks with laughter.
"I know,"
it whispers.
"The whole forest knows."
It gets up at once, the squirrel clinging on, and bows you past.
In the middle of the worst glade sits a humming gem the size of a fist. Every tree leans away.
"Mend the glade, and the stone sinks back into the ground,"
says the Elder Unicorn.
"Take it, and the glade never mends."
Everybody vote.
"Sorry,"
you tell the oak.
"We're keeping it."
A long creak, like somebody thinking. Then one leaf drifts onto your pocket, right over the stone, like a label. The forest will remember who has it.
You camp at the northern edge of the Woods, on moss soft as a pillow. At dusk the MossHome runner jogs by.
"MossHome's just north!"
All night a mosshorn guards your fire. The forest has marked you present.
You camp at the northern edge of the Woods. At dusk the MossHome runner jogs by.
"MossHome's just north!"
The Glade Stone hums all night, and no mosshorn comes near. Next to your name, the forest wrote something you can't read.

When you find your way back, the worst glade is already green. The unicorns mended it without you. The forest walks you to its northern edge, like a guest to the door. At dusk the MossHome runner waves.
"MossHome's just north!"
A young unicorn steps out of the ferns with a leaf full of spring water. You carry it together to a thirsty glade without spilling a drop.
"For later,"
she says, handing you a tiny bottle of sunbloom nectar.
You press a coin into the squirrel's paw. It bites the coin and whispers in the beech's ear.
"Fine,"
creaks the beech, shuffling aside. The squirrel hands you a plum-sized acorn. "Throw it hard. It goes bang."
